**Short answer**

- The Ajuran Empire fought off Portuguese incursions and, in the process, “expelled” or drove out the Europeans and any local groups that had been complicit with them.  
- In a very different part of the world, the construction of the Nam Tha dam ( “Tha” is the Lao word for “river” – the dam is usually called the Nam Tha Hydropower Plant) on the Lao‑Thai border has **forced the removal of more than 10 000 ethnic‑Lao and minority‑people** from their ancestral villages.  The people were resettled in government‑built “resettlement towns” or deprived of their land and livelihoods, a process that has been described as an expulsion from the natural boundary that the Mekong River forms between Thailand and Laos.

---

### 1.  The Ajuran Empire: a “self‑declared independence” from the Portuguese

| What happened | How it happened | Source |
|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| **The Ajuran Sultanate (13th‑17th C.)** was a Somali Muslim state that at its height controlled trade and water‑management on the lower Juba and Shebelle rivers, and the coasts of Mogadishu, Barawa and Merca. | **Military campaigns against the Portuguese** – the Ajuran raided Portuguese trading ships, blockaded the harbour at Mogadishu, and fought at the Battle of Benadir (1589 C.) – forced the Portuguese to abandon most of their coastal holdings in the Horn of Africa. | Wikipedia – *Ajuran Sultanate*; “Ajuran‑Portuguese battles” section. |
| **“Expulsion” of the Portuguese** – the Ajuran also pushed back any local or foreign traders who had allied with the Portuguese and seized Portuguese‑built forts. | The Ajuran used a mix of naval manoeuvres, fortified coastal walls and an army that could shift quickly between sea and land, which led to a **complete expulsion of Portuguese forces** from coastal Somalia by the late‑16th C. | Same Wikipedia info; “Ajuran‐Portuguese battles” with reference to the Battle of Benadir. |
| The expulsion was followed by a **re‑assertion of Islamic law and local clan sovereignty** across the empire. | The merchants that had been educated in Ottoman, Portuguese or Arab trade were forced to abandon foreign trading practices and adopt the Ajuran system of *saddax* tax – effectively a local tax collected in exchange for water‑management services. | Same source. |

> *“The Somali‑Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. … The Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India, and the Portuguese armada then retook most of the lost cities.”* – *Ajuran Sultanate* Wikipedia (notable for showing the aggressive expulsion of a foreign power).|

---

### 2.  The Nam Tha dam on the Thai‑Laos border

| What happened | Why it is an “expulsion” | Key figures | Source |
|---------------|--------------------------|--------------|--------|
| **The Nam Tha hydropower plant (first phase)** was built in the early‑2010s by a subsidiary of China Southern Power Grid on the Tha (Nam Tha) River, a tributary that joins the Mekong just south of the Thai‑Laos border. | **Displacement of thousands of people** – the reservoir will submerge villages and farmland; the Lao government is forced to relocate residents to new “resettlement towns.” | ~10 000 ethnic‑Lao and minority people are displaced; about 7 000 will be moved to a new town called “Ban Hadmuark.” | – “Damming the Nam Tha in Northern Laos” – The Diplomat (June 2016) – “Nam Tha dam will displace over 10 000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples”. |
| **The rapids of the river are originally a natural boundary** between Thailand and Laos (the Mekong itself).  The dam breaks that natural “border” by blocking the flow and flooding upstream villages. | Although the dam is in Laos, the **displaced people** are those who once lived along the entire riverbank – some of whom have cultural ties to communities on the Thai side.  The dam’s construction effectively forces them “out of their homes” and **outside the built‑environment corridor** that previously served cross‑border trade and movement. | Government of Laos & China Southern Power Grid (planning agencies). | – Same article above; also Open Development Mekong – *“Nam Tha dam will displace over 10 000 ethnic Lao…”* |
| **Resettlement efforts** involve building new homes, schools, and a “resettlement town.”  Many villagers claim that their cultural and agricultural practices are disrupted, and that the new settlement is not a comparable replacement. | The forced relocation is described by local NGOs and journalists as an **expulsion** from the area that used to be a natural landscape spanning both sides of the river. | Lao People’s Revolutionary Party officials; local NGOs, e.g., International Rivers. | – The same Diplomat article and other NGO reports. |

> *“…the Nam Tha dam is being built … 95 per cent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. … Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10 000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples.”* – *The Diplomat*.

---

### 3.  Connection – why the question compares the two

* In both cases the indigenous community was **pushed away from a natural boundary** (the Somali coast against the Portuguese, and the lower Mekong at the Thai‑Laos border).  
* The **Ajuran** side represents a *military expulsion* of an occupying foreign power; the **Nam Tha** side represents a *political‑economic expulsion* of local people by a modern state backed by foreign investment.  
* Both situations involved a **first wave of removal** followed by **resettlement or loss of land**.

---

### 4.  Bottom line

| Ajuran Empire | Nam Tha dam |
|------------------------|--------------|
| **Expelled the Portuguese** by force; expelled those who collaborated with them. | **Expelled over 10 000 ethnic‑Lao** by flooding their villages for a hydroelectric plant. |
| Expulsion through **battle and capture of coastal bases**. | Expulsion through **construction and forced relocation**. |
| Resulted in **re‑assertion of Somali Muslim sovereignty**. | Resulted in **loss of ancestral lands and altered livelihoods**. |

Both cases are examples of how a larger political or economic coalition (a medieval Somali empire or a modern Lao government backed by China) can forcefully remove people from a natural border area and re‑design the region for its own purposes.

##### Description
Khun Dan Dam was built according to the King’s project. The King had royally given the name of the dam as Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam to honor the bravery of Khun Han Phithak Phraiwan or Khun Dan, the hero of Nakhon Nayok in the Ayutthaya era. The dam is 2,720 meters long, 93 meters high and can contain water for 224 million cubic meters. It receives the water that flows from Khao Yai National Park through Heo Narok Waterfall into the reservoir. It can prevent flooding and reduce the damage from overflowing. It is a new tourist attraction of Nakhon Nayok in which you can see the view of Khao Yai National Park from the ridge of the dam and see the landscape of Mueang Nakhon Nayok from behind the dam.
* * *

##### History
Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam, the Royal Projects The King had considered on 4 December 1993 on the occasion of the King’s Birthday and had royally given order to the Royal Irrigation Department to lay the project and construct the Khlong Tha Dan Dam at Ban Tha Dan, Hin Tung Sub-District, Mueang district, Nakhon Nayok province. It is a part of the basin development project in the basin of the upper part of Nakhon Nayok to help the people in the lower part to have the water for agriculture use and consumption as well as mitigate the flooding that often occurs in the area of Nakhon Nayok province annually for industry and to correct the problem of acid soil. Objective: 1. To be the water source that can allocate the water into the irrigation area of 185,000 rai with the previous Tha Dan project of 6,000 rai, the extension part of Tha Dan project of 14,000 rai, and Nakhon Nayok water transmission and maintenance project of 165,000 rai 2. To be the water source for consumption and industry 3. To mitigate the flooding in the area of Nakhon Nayok province 4. To correct the problem of acid soil in Nakhon Nayok province 1) Headwork Dam and Buildings, which consist of (1) Main Dam It is the Roller Compacted Concrete or RCC Dam with the height of 93 meters, the dam ridge level of +112 m. msl., the length of 2,594 meters, and the volume of roller compacted concrete of 5,470,000 cubic meters. (2) Spillway It is the reinforced concrete that can drain the highest amount of water of 1,454 cubic meters/second through 4 vents in the form of weir at the level of +103.50 m. msl., which is controlled by 4 sets of Radial Gate in the size of 10.00 x 8.40 meters per set.

##### History
(3) River Outlet It is the reinforced concrete that can control the flow rate by using Fixed Wheel Gate in the size of 2.00 x 5.00 meters and Butterfly Valve with the diameter size of 2.0 meters and the pipe sill level of +28.50 m. msl. through the iron pipe with the diameter size of 2.0 meters. It is also able to drain into the downstream by Hollow Jet Valve Øof 1.80 meter, which can drain water for 42 cubic meters/second. (4) Bottom Outlet It is the reinforced concrete with the sill level of +29.00 m. msl., draining through the channel in the size of 5.0 meters wide and 3.0 meter high, controlling the flow by Fixed Wheel Gate in the size of 2.50 x 3.90 meters, and Radial Gate in the size of 2.50 x 3.45 meters that can drain water at 182.0 cubic meters/second, which can reduce the water from the retention water level of +110.00 m. msl. down to the level of +70.00 m. msl. within 10 days. (5) Irrigation Outlet It is the reinforced concrete that drains the water through the stainless pipe in the diameter size of 0.90 meter with the sill level of +38.45 m. msl., controlling the flow by Fixed Wheel Gate and Butterfly Valve with the diameter size of 0.70 meter in the number of 2 sets, draining the water into the irrigation canal by Hollow Jet Valve with the diameter size of 0.70 meter (2 sets) and able to deliver the water into the canal in the total volume of 6.05 cubic meters/second. (6) Diversion Building during the Dam Construction, which consists of The soiled barrage that obstructs the existing watercourse with the height of 12.00 meters, the barrage ridge level of +39.00 m. msl., the width of 5.00 meters, and the total length of 1,084 meters. The Retaining Wall concrete building on the upstream and downstream with the height of 12.00 meters and 13.00 meters, respectively.

##### History
The 2-channel reinforced concrete diversion building in the size of 7.00 x 9.00 meters and 6.00 x 9.00 meters, which is able to drain the water at 700 cubic meters/second (Return Period of 20 years) with the sill level of +27.00 m. msl. (7) Saddle Dam It is a soiled dam that is 46.0 meters high with the dam ridge at the level of +114 m. msl., the width of 8.0 meters, the length of 350 meters, the dam volume of 1,220,000 cubic meters. 2) Distribution System and Drainage System, which consist of (1) The area of the existing and the extension Tha Dam project in the total of 20,000 rai (2) The area of Nakhon Nayok Distribution and Maintenance System of 165,000 rai Acquired Benefits: 1. Distribute the water for agricultural in the area in the total of 185,000 rai 2. Distribute the water for consumption of 16 million cubic meters per year 3. Farmers receive the benefits for 5,400 households. 4. Mitigate the problem of acid soil 5. Reduce the damage from flooding for 35 percent It is the headwork dam construction project and buildings that consist of other components with a reservoir capacity of 224 million cubic meters with a reservoir surface at the normal retention level of 3,087 rai.

Leaflet | © OpenStreetMap contributors.
The Nam Tha, or Tha River, begins in northern Laos near the Lao-China border and runs southwest to join the Mekong just south of Huay Xay on the Lao-Thai border. In October 2014, I traveled by motorcycle and longtail boat up the Nam Tha, starting from its mouth at Pak Tha, to investigate a dam project on the river. The Nam Tha dam is being built by a subsidiary of the China Southern Power Grid, and 95 percent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10,000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples.

The Nam Tha, or Tha River, begins in northern Laos near the Lao-China border and runs southwest to join the Mekong just south of Huay Xay on the Lao-Thai border. In October 2014, I traveled by motorcycle and longtail boat up the Nam Tha, starting from its mouth at Pak Tha, to investigate a dam project on the river. The Nam Tha dam is being built by a subsidiary of the China Southern Power Grid, and 95 percent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10,000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples.

##### Description
Khun Dan Dam was built according to the King’s project. The King had royally given the name of the dam as Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam to honor the bravery of Khun Han Phithak Phraiwan or Khun Dan, the hero of Nakhon Nayok in the Ayutthaya era. The dam is 2,720 meters long, 93 meters high and can contain water for 224 million cubic meters. It receives the water that flows from Khao Yai National Park through Heo Narok Waterfall into the reservoir. It can prevent flooding and reduce the damage from overflowing. It is a new tourist attraction of Nakhon Nayok in which you can see the view of Khao Yai National Park from the ridge of the dam and see the landscape of Mueang Nakhon Nayok from behind the dam.
* * *
texts.1:
##### History
Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam, the Royal Projects The King had considered on 4 December 1993 on the occasion of the King’s Birthday and had royally given order to the Royal Irrigation Department to lay the project and construct the Khlong Tha Dan Dam at Ban Tha Dan, Hin Tung Sub-District, Mueang district, Nakhon Nayok province. It is a part of the basin development project in the basin of the upper part of Nakhon Nayok to help the people in the lower part to have the water for agriculture use and consumption as well as mitigate the flooding that often occurs in the area of Nakhon Nayok province annually for industry and to correct the problem of acid soil. Objective: 1. To be the water source that can allocate the water into the irrigation area of 185,000 rai with the previous Tha Dan project of 6,000 rai, the extension part of Tha Dan project of 14,000 rai, and Nakhon Nayok water transmission and maintenance project of 165,000 rai 2. To be the water source for consumption and industry 3. To mitigate the flooding in the area of Nakhon Nayok province 4. To correct the problem of acid soil in Nakhon Nayok province 1) Headwork Dam and Buildings, which consist of (1) Main Dam It is the Roller Compacted Concrete or RCC Dam with the height of 93 meters, the dam ridge level of +112 m. msl., the length of 2,594 meters, and the volume of roller compacted concrete of 5,470,000 cubic meters. (2) Spillway It is the reinforced concrete that can drain the highest amount of water of 1,454 cubic meters/second through 4 vents in the form of weir at the level of +103.50 m. msl., which is controlled by 4 sets of Radial Gate in the size of 10.00 x 8.40 meters per set.
texts.2:

It is also able to drain into the downstream by Hollow Jet Valve Øof 1.80 meter, which can drain water for 42 cubic meters/second. ##### Description
Khun Dan Dam was built according to the King’s project. The King had royally given the name of the dam as Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam to honor the bravery of Khun Han Phithak Phraiwan or Khun Dan, the hero of Nakhon Nayok in the Ayutthaya era. The dam is 2,720 meters long, 93 meters high and can contain water for 224 million cubic meters. It receives the water that flows from Khao Yai National Park through Heo Narok Waterfall into the reservoir. It can prevent flooding and reduce the damage from overflowing. It is a new tourist attraction of Nakhon Nayok in which you can see the view of Khao Yai National Park from the ridge of the dam and see the landscape of Mueang Nakhon Nayok from behind the dam.
* * *

##### History
Khun Dan Prakan Chon Dam, the Royal Projects The King had considered on 4 December 1993 on the occasion of the King’s Birthday and had royally given order to the Royal Irrigation Department to lay the project and construct the Khlong Tha Dan Dam at Ban Tha Dan, Hin Tung Sub-District, Mueang district, Nakhon Nayok province. It is a part of the basin development project in the basin of the upper part of Nakhon Nayok to help the people in the lower part to have the water for agriculture use and consumption as well as mitigate the flooding that often occurs in the area of Nakhon Nayok province annually for industry and to correct the problem of acid soil. Objective: 1. To be the water source that can allocate the water into the irrigation area of 185,000 rai with the previous Tha Dan project of 6,000 rai, the extension part of Tha Dan project of 14,000 rai, and Nakhon Nayok water transmission and maintenance project of 165,000 rai 2. To be the water source for consumption and industry 3. To mitigate the flooding in the area of Nakhon Nayok province 4. To correct the problem of acid soil in Nakhon Nayok province 1) Headwork Dam and Buildings, which consist of (1) Main Dam It is the Roller Compacted Concrete or RCC Dam with the height of 93 meters, the dam ridge level of +112 m. msl., the length of 2,594 meters, and the volume of roller compacted concrete of 5,470,000 cubic meters. (2) Spillway It is the reinforced concrete that can drain the highest amount of water of 1,454 cubic meters/second through 4 vents in the form of weir at the level of +103.50 m. msl., which is controlled by 4 sets of Radial Gate in the size of 10.00 x 8.40 meters per set.

It is also able to drain into the downstream by Hollow Jet Valve Øof 1.80 meter, which can drain water for 42 cubic meters/second. ### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

## Chronological Chapters
### Ibn Battuta’s Chronicling of Mogadishu
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The legendary Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visits Mogadishu, documenting its immense wealth, scholarly culture, and legal system.
In 1331 CE, the legendary Moroccan scholar and explorer Ibn Battuta arrived in Mogadishu during his extensive travels across the Islamic world. His detailed, first-hand chronicle provides modern historians with an invaluable window into the zenith of the Mogadishu Sultanate, confirming its status as an exceptionally wealthy, orderly, and cosmopolitan metropolis.
Upon his arrival, Ibn Battuta was struck by the sheer scale of the city's commerce. He described Mogadishu as 'a town of enormous size' filled with rich merchants. He noted that the city was famous for its vast herds of camels and sheep, and its massive export of textiles to Egypt and beyond. He was formally received by the Sultan, Abu Bakr ibn Sayx 'Umar, who spoke both Somali (referred to by Battuta as the local dialect) and Arabic. Ibn Battuta was highly impressed by the sophisticated court etiquette, where the Sultan was accompanied by Islamic jurists, wazirs, and military commanders.
The traveler detailed the city's culinary traditions, noting the abundance of rice cooked with ghee, served with side dishes of meat, chicken, and fish, and accompanied by unripe bananas and sour milk. More importantly, he highlighted the high level of Islamic scholarship and legal sophistication in Mogadishu, describing a well-organized judicial system based on the Shafi'i school of jurisprudence. Ibn Battuta's writings served as a primary historical record that integrated Somalia into the broader narrative of the medieval Islamic Golden Age, proving that the Horn of Africa was not a marginal periphery, but a highly sophisticated center of global civilization.

### The Golden Age of the Ajuran Sultanate
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The Ajuran Sultanate establishes a highly centralized hydraulic empire, dominating Somali trade and agriculture.
During the 13th to 17th centuries, the Ajuran Sultanate ruled over vast swaths of southern Somalia. Unlike many decentralized contemporary societies, the Ajuran established a highly centralized, militarized, and sophisticated state. It is best remembered in African history as a hydraulic empire, utilizing advanced water management systems to assert control over agricultural land and nomadic trade routes.
The Ajuran state, led by the Gareen dynasty, constructed an extensive network of limestone wells, cisterns, and canals along the Shebelle and Jubba rivers. This stable revenue funded a professional standing army, centralized administration, and monumental construction projects, including stone castles, fortresses, and defensive walls that still dot the Somali landscape today.
The Ajuran also dominated maritime trade, aligning with coastal city-states like Mogadishu, Merca, and Barawa. Their naval and land forces successfully resisted Portuguese expansion in the western Indian Ocean, protecting Somali independence. Under Ajuran rule, the region experienced a golden age of stability, architectural innovation, and agricultural wealth, demonstrating a unique synthesis of engineering prowess and absolute political authority.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Adal-Ethiopian War
#### Historical Sites & Locations
Imam Ahmad al-Ghazi of the Adal Sultanate launches a massive invasion of the Ethiopian Empire, altering Horn of Africa geopolitics.
In the early 16th century, long-standing religious, economic, and territorial tensions between the Muslim Adal Sultanate (headquartered in Zeila, northern Somalia) and the Christian Solomonic Empire of Ethiopia erupted into a devastating, total conflict. Led by the charismatic military commander Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, famously known as 'Ahmad Gurey' (the Left-Handed), the Adal Sultanate launched a massive holy war (jihad) in 1529, aiming to conquer the Ethiopian highlands.
Imam Ahmad revolutionized warfare in the region by securing matchlock muskets and military advisors from the Ottoman Empire, giving his forces a decisive technological advantage over the traditional Ethiopian armies. With a multi-ethnic coalition of Somali, Afar, and Harari warriors, Ahmad Gurey swept through the Ethiopian Empire. His forces captured royal strongholds, destroyed ancient Christian monasteries, and conquered nearly three-quarters of Ethiopia, forcing the Ethiopian Emperor Dawit II (and later Gelawdewos) into hiding.
Facing existential collapse, the Ethiopian crown appealed to Portugal for aid. In 1541, a Portuguese expeditionary force commanded by Cristóvão da Gama arrived with advanced firearms and artillery. The conflict escalated into a global proxy war between the Ottoman and Portuguese empires. In 1543, at the decisive Battle of Wayna Daga, a combined Portuguese-Ethiopian force defeated the Adal army, and Imam Ahmad was killed in action. The war ended with both empires utterly exhausted, leaving a legacy of deep-seated religious and territorial rivalry that would shape Horn of Africa geopolitics for half a millennium.

### The Battle of Benadir
#### Historical Sites & Locations
Ajuran forces and Ottoman allies decisively defeat Portuguese attempts to conquer the Somali coast.
In the late 16th century, the Portuguese Empire sought to establish a total monopoly over the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Having successfully captured coastal cities in India and East Africa (such as Mombasa), the Portuguese turned their sights toward the wealthy Somali trade ports of the Benadir coast, including Mogadishu, Barawa, and Merca, which were aligned with the Ajuran Sultanate.
In 1589, a Portuguese fleet under the command of João de Lodi attempted a major naval assault and blockade on the Somali coast. The Ajuran Sultanate, demonstrating remarkable military coordination, mobilized its land forces and allied with Ottoman corsairs led by the famous admiral Mir Ali Bey. The Ottomans provided crucial naval support and artillery, while Ajuran soldiers defended the coastal cities from land-based incursions.
The Battle of Benadir resulted in a decisive victory for the Somali-Ottoman alliance. The Portuguese were repelled with heavy casualties, and several of their ships were captured or destroyed. This battle effectively halted Portuguese colonial ambitions along the Somali coast, preserving the sovereignty and trade independence of the Somali city-states. It highlighted the Ajuran Sultanate's capacity to engage in high-stakes global diplomacy and warfare, maintaining the Horn of Africa as a free zone for Islamic and Asian trade.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Rise of the Geledi Sultanate
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The Geledi Sultanate defeats the oppressive Silis dynasty, establishing hegemony over the southern Somali interior.
Following the decline of the Ajuran Sultanate, southern Somalia experienced a period of political fragmentation and local oppression. In the early 18th century, the Silis dynasty, based in Afgooye, established a highly tyrannical rule over the local population, extracting heavy taxes and enforcing cruel laws. This sparked a popular rebellion led by the Geledi clan, a branch of the Rahanweyn Somalis.
Under the brilliant leadership of Ibrahim Adeer, the Geledi successfully defeated the Silis forces, liberating Afgooye and laying the foundation for the Geledi Sultanate. Ibrahim Adeer established a highly sophisticated, constitutional monarchy that balanced the interests of various Somali clans and agricultural communities along the Jubba and Shebelle rivers. The Sultanate reached its absolute zenith in the mid-19th century under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim.
The Geledi Sultanate was a major economic power, controlling the lucrative ivory, leather, and agricultural trade of the interior, and channeling it to coastal ports like Mogadishu and Barawa. In 1843, the Geledi army decisively defeated a major rebellion by the Bardera Jihadists, securing their hegemony. The Geledi era proved that Somali political institutions could adapt, innovate, and thrive, creating a prosperous, decentralized federal system that respected local clan autonomy while maintaining regional peace and immense commercial wealth.

Led by the charismatic military commander Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, famously known as 'Ahmad Gurey' (the Left-Handed), the Adal Sultanate launched a massive holy war (jihad) in 1529, aiming to conquer the Ethiopian highlands.
Imam Ahmad revolutionized warfare in the region by securing matchlock muskets and military advisors from the Ottoman Empire, giving his forces a decisive technological advantage over the traditional Ethiopian armies. With a multi-ethnic coalition of Somali, Afar, and Harari warriors, Ahmad Gurey swept through the Ethiopian Empire. His forces captured royal strongholds, destroyed ancient Christian monasteries, and conquered nearly three-quarters of Ethiopia, forcing the Ethiopian Emperor Dawit II (and later Gelawdewos) into hiding.
Facing existential collapse, the Ethiopian crown appealed to Portugal for aid. In 1541, a Portuguese expeditionary force commanded by Cristóvão da Gama arrived with advanced firearms and artillery. The conflict escalated into a global proxy war between the Ottoman and Portuguese empires. In 1543, at the decisive Battle of Wayna Daga, a combined Portuguese-Ethiopian force defeated the Adal army, and Imam Ahmad was killed in action. The war ended with both empires utterly exhausted, leaving a legacy of deep-seated religious and territorial rivalry that would shape Horn of Africa geopolitics for half a millennium.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Battle of Benadir
#### Historical Sites & Locations
Ajuran forces and Ottoman allies decisively defeat Portuguese attempts to conquer the Somali coast.
In the late 16th century, the Portuguese Empire sought to establish a total monopoly over the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Having successfully captured coastal cities in India and East Africa (such as Mombasa), the Portuguese turned their sights toward the wealthy Somali trade ports of the Benadir coast, including Mogadishu, Barawa, and Merca, which were aligned with the Ajuran Sultanate.
In 1589, a Portuguese fleet under the command of João de Lodi attempted a major naval assault and blockade on the Somali coast. The Ajuran Sultanate, demonstrating remarkable military coordination, mobilized its land forces and allied with Ottoman corsairs led by the famous admiral Mir Ali Bey. The Ottomans provided crucial naval support and artillery, while Ajuran soldiers defended the coastal cities from land-based incursions.
The Battle of Benadir resulted in a decisive victory for the Somali-Ottoman alliance. The Portuguese were repelled with heavy casualties, and several of their ships were captured or destroyed. This battle effectively halted Portuguese colonial ambitions along the Somali coast, preserving the sovereignty and trade independence of the Somali city-states. It highlighted the Ajuran Sultanate's capacity to engage in high-stakes global diplomacy and warfare, maintaining the Horn of Africa as a free zone for Islamic and Asian trade.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Rise of the Geledi Sultanate
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The Geledi Sultanate defeats the oppressive Silis dynasty, establishing hegemony over the southern Somali interior.
Following the decline of the Ajuran Sultanate, southern Somalia experienced a period of political fragmentation and local oppression. In the early 18th century, the Silis dynasty, based in Afgooye, established a highly tyrannical rule over the local population, extracting heavy taxes and enforcing cruel laws. This sparked a popular rebellion led by the Geledi clan, a branch of the Rahanweyn Somalis.
Under the brilliant leadership of Ibrahim Adeer, the Geledi successfully defeated the Silis forces, liberating Afgooye and laying the foundation for the Geledi Sultanate. Ibrahim Adeer established a highly sophisticated, constitutional monarchy that balanced the interests of various Somali clans and agricultural communities along the Jubba and Shebelle rivers. The Sultanate reached its absolute zenith in the mid-19th century under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim.
The Geledi Sultanate was a major economic power, controlling the lucrative ivory, leather, and agricultural trade of the interior, and channeling it to coastal ports like Mogadishu and Barawa. In 1843, the Geledi army decisively defeated a major rebellion by the Bardera Jihadists, securing their hegemony. The Geledi era proved that Somali political institutions could adapt, innovate, and thrive, creating a prosperous, decentralized federal system that respected local clan autonomy while maintaining regional peace and immense commercial wealth.

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

The tomb of Sheikh Hussein

The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)

## Chronological Chapters
### Ibn Battuta’s Chronicling of Mogadishu
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The legendary Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visits Mogadishu, documenting its immense wealth, scholarly culture, and legal system.
In 1331 CE, the legendary Moroccan scholar and explorer Ibn Battuta arrived in Mogadishu during his extensive travels across the Islamic world. His detailed, first-hand chronicle provides modern historians with an invaluable window into the zenith of the Mogadishu Sultanate, confirming its status as an exceptionally wealthy, orderly, and cosmopolitan metropolis.
Upon his arrival, Ibn Battuta was struck by the sheer scale of the city's commerce. He described Mogadishu as 'a town of enormous size' filled with rich merchants. He noted that the city was famous for its vast herds of camels and sheep, and its massive export of textiles to Egypt and beyond. He was formally received by the Sultan, Abu Bakr ibn Sayx 'Umar, who spoke both Somali (referred to by Battuta as the local dialect) and Arabic. Ibn Battuta was highly impressed by the sophisticated court etiquette, where the Sultan was accompanied by Islamic jurists, wazirs, and military commanders.
The traveler detailed the city's culinary traditions, noting the abundance of rice cooked with ghee, served with side dishes of meat, chicken, and fish, and accompanied by unripe bananas and sour milk. More importantly, he highlighted the high level of Islamic scholarship and legal sophistication in Mogadishu, describing a well-organized judicial system based on the Shafi'i school of jurisprudence. Ibn Battuta's writings served as a primary historical record that integrated Somalia into the broader narrative of the medieval Islamic Golden Age, proving that the Horn of Africa was not a marginal periphery, but a highly sophisticated center of global civilization.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Golden Age of the Ajuran Sultanate
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The Ajuran Sultanate establishes a highly centralized hydraulic empire, dominating Somali trade and agriculture.
During the 13th to 17th centuries, the Ajuran Sultanate ruled over vast swaths of southern Somalia. Unlike many decentralized contemporary societies, the Ajuran established a highly centralized, militarized, and sophisticated state. It is best remembered in African history as a hydraulic empire, utilizing advanced water management systems to assert control over agricultural land and nomadic trade routes.
The Ajuran state, led by the Gareen dynasty, constructed an extensive network of limestone wells, cisterns, and canals along the Shebelle and Jubba rivers. By monopolizing access to water in the arid Horn of Africa, the Ajuran rulers extracted taxes (known as 'Saddax') from nomadic pastoralists and agriculturalists alike. This stable revenue funded a professional standing army, centralized administration, and monumental construction projects, including stone castles, fortresses, and defensive walls that still dot the Somali landscape today.
The Ajuran also dominated maritime trade, aligning with coastal city-states like Mogadishu, Merca, and Barawa. Their naval and land forces successfully resisted Portuguese expansion in the western Indian Ocean, protecting Somali independence. Under Ajuran rule, the region experienced a golden age of stability, architectural innovation, and agricultural wealth, demonstrating a unique synthesis of engineering prowess and absolute political authority.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Adal-Ethiopian War
#### Historical Sites & Locations
Imam Ahmad al-Ghazi of the Adal Sultanate launches a massive invasion of the Ethiopian Empire, altering Horn of Africa geopolitics.
In the early 16th century, long-standing religious, economic, and territorial tensions between the Muslim Adal Sultanate (headquartered in Zeila, northern Somalia) and the Christian Solomonic Empire of Ethiopia erupted into a devastating, total conflict. Led by the charismatic military commander Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, famously known as 'Ahmad Gurey' (the Left-Handed), the Adal Sultanate launched a massive holy war (jihad) in 1529, aiming to conquer the Ethiopian highlands.
Imam Ahmad revolutionized warfare in the region by securing matchlock muskets and military advisors from the Ottoman Empire, giving his forces a decisive technological advantage over the traditional Ethiopian armies. With a multi-ethnic coalition of Somali, Afar, and Harari warriors, Ahmad Gurey swept through the Ethiopian Empire. His forces captured royal strongholds, destroyed ancient Christian monasteries, and conquered nearly three-quarters of Ethiopia, forcing the Ethiopian Emperor Dawit II (and later Gelawdewos) into hiding.
Facing existential collapse, the Ethiopian crown appealed to Portugal for aid. In 1541, a Portuguese expeditionary force commanded by Cristóvão da Gama arrived with advanced firearms and artillery. The conflict escalated into a global proxy war between the Ottoman and Portuguese empires. In 1543, at the decisive Battle of Wayna Daga, a combined Portuguese-Ethiopian force defeated the Adal army, and Imam Ahmad was killed in action. The war ended with both empires utterly exhausted, leaving a legacy of deep-seated religious and territorial rivalry that would shape Horn of Africa geopolitics for half a millennium.

### The Battle of Benadir
#### Historical Sites & Locations
Ajuran forces and Ottoman allies decisively defeat Portuguese attempts to conquer the Somali coast.
In the late 16th century, the Portuguese Empire sought to establish a total monopoly over the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Having successfully captured coastal cities in India and East Africa (such as Mombasa), the Portuguese turned their sights toward the wealthy Somali trade ports of the Benadir coast, including Mogadishu, Barawa, and Merca, which were aligned with the Ajuran Sultanate.
In 1589, a Portuguese fleet under the command of João de Lodi attempted a major naval assault and blockade on the Somali coast. The Ajuran Sultanate, demonstrating remarkable military coordination, mobilized its land forces and allied with Ottoman corsairs led by the famous admiral Mir Ali Bey. The Ottomans provided crucial naval support and artillery, while Ajuran soldiers defended the coastal cities from land-based incursions.
The Battle of Benadir resulted in a decisive victory for the Somali-Ottoman alliance. The Portuguese were repelled with heavy casualties, and several of their ships were captured or destroyed. This battle effectively halted Portuguese colonial ambitions along the Somali coast, preserving the sovereignty and trade independence of the Somali city-states. It highlighted the Ajuran Sultanate's capacity to engage in high-stakes global diplomacy and warfare, maintaining the Horn of Africa as a free zone for Islamic and Asian trade.

## Chronological Chapters
### The Rise of the Geledi Sultanate
#### Historical Sites & Locations
The Geledi Sultanate defeats the oppressive Silis dynasty, establishing hegemony over the southern Somali interior.
Following the decline of the Ajuran Sultanate, southern Somalia experienced a period of political fragmentation and local oppression. In the early 18th century, the Silis dynasty, based in Afgooye, established a highly tyrannical rule over the local population, extracting heavy taxes and enforcing cruel laws. This sparked a popular rebellion led by the Geledi clan, a branch of the Rahanweyn Somalis.
Under the brilliant leadership of Ibrahim Adeer, the Geledi successfully defeated the Silis forces, liberating Afgooye and laying the foundation for the Geledi Sultanate. Ibrahim Adeer established a highly sophisticated, constitutional monarchy that balanced the interests of various Somali clans and agricultural communities along the Jubba and Shebelle rivers. The Sultanate reached its absolute zenith in the mid-19th century under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim.
The Geledi Sultanate was a major economic power, controlling the lucrative ivory, leather, and agricultural trade of the interior, and channeling it to coastal ports like Mogadishu and Barawa. In 1843, the Geledi army decisively defeated a major rebellion by the Bardera Jihadists, securing their hegemony. The Geledi era proved that Somali political institutions could adapt, innovate, and thrive, creating a prosperous, decentralized federal system that respected local clan autonomy while maintaining regional peace and immense commercial wealth.

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
Over the next decades tensions remained high and the increased contact between Somali sailors and Ottomancorsairs worried the Portuguese who sent a punitive expedition under João de Sepúlveda, where he bombarded Mogadishu and captured Turkish vessels, compelling its ruler to sign a peace deal with the Portuguese. Barawa would also sign peace with the Portuguese after being sacked.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Sep%C3%BAlveda,_1542-53) The Ottoman-Somali cooperation against the Portuguese on the Indian Ocean reached a high point in the 1580s when Ajuran clients of the coastal cities began to cooperate with the Arabs and Swahilis under Portuguese rule and sent an envoy to the Turkish corsair Mir Ali Bey for a joint expedition against the Portuguese. He agreed and was joined by a Somali fleet in order to attack the Portuguese colonies in Southeast Africa.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWelch195025-54)
A 16th century map by Jan Huyghen[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-55)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
The Somali-Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. However, the Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India requesting a large Portuguese fleet. This request was answered and it reversed the previous offensive of the Muslims into one of defense. The Portuguese armada managed to re-take most of the lost cities and began punishing their leaders, but they refrained from attacking Mogadishu, securing the city's autonomy in the Indian Ocean.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Cites-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-57) The Ottoman Empire would remain an economic partner.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Shapes-12) Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries the Ajurans successively defied Portuguese hegemony on the Indian Ocean by employing a new coinage which followed the Ottoman pattern, thus proclaiming an attitude of economic independence in regard to the Portuguese.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-61)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
From the late 15th and up until the 17th centuries saw the arrival of Muslim families from Arabia, Persia, India and Spain to the Ajuran realm of territories, the majority of whom settled in the coastal provinces. Some migrated because of the instability in their respective regions, as was the case with the Hadhrami families from Yemen and Muslims from Spain fleeing the Inquisition.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-63) Others came to conduct business or for religious purposes. Due to their strong tradition in religious learning, the new Muslim communities also enjoyed high status among the Somali ruling elite and commoners.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-65)
The tomb of Sheikh Hussein
The most famous Somali scholar of Islam from the Ajuraan period is Sheikh Hussein, who was born in Merca, one of the power jurisdiction and cultural centers of the Ajuran Empire.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-66) He is credited with converting the Sidamo people living in the area of what is now the Bale Province, Ethiopia to Islam.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-67) He is also credited with establishing the Sultanate of Bale.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-69)
Despite the Bale Sultanate not being directly under Ajuran rule, the two kingdoms were deeply connected and Bale was heavily influenced by Ajuran. His tomb lies in the town of Sheikh Hussein in what is considered the most sacred place in the country for Ethiopian Muslims, in particular those of Oromo ethnic descent.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-71)

### Ajuran-Portuguese battles
In the mid-17th century, the Oromo people collectively began expanding from their homeland towards the southern Somali coast at a time when the Ajurans were at the height of their power.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECassanelli1982114-72) The Garen rulers conducted several military expeditions known as the _Gaal Madow_ _Wars,_ on the Oromo invaders, converting those that were captured to Islam.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-76)

### Fall of Benadir and Southern Somalia
[edit]
The Ajuran Empire slowly declined in power at the end of the 17th century. In this period the rulers of the empire abandoned Sharia, became oppressive and enacted heavy taxation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:4-9) The dethronement of the Muzaffar clients in Mogadishu and other coastal cities by the Abgaalimam who then established the Hiraab Imamate taking residence in Mogadishu was a significant setback,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis198837-77) and the defeat of the Silcis vassals by a former Ajuran general in the interior of the state, Ibrahim Adeer, who established the Gobroon dynasty.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) By the early 1700s there was effectively no trace of Ajuran left in Banaadir.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-:3-25)
Taxation and the practice of primae noctis were the main catalysts for the revolts against Ajuran rulers.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-80) The loss of port cities and fertile farms meant that much needed sources of revenue were lost to the rebels.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-Lewis_1960_213%E2%80%93230-79) Somali maritime enterprise significantly declined after the collapse of the Ajuran Empire. However, other principalities such as the Isaaq Sultanate, Warsangali Sultanate, Majeerteen Sultanate, and the Sultanate of Hobyo in a way ensured its continuity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajuran_Sultanate#cite_note-81)

The Nam Tha, or Tha River, begins in northern Laos near the Lao-China border and runs southwest to join the Mekong just south of Huay Xay on the Lao-Thai border. In October 2014, I traveled by motorcycle and longtail boat up the Nam Tha, starting from its mouth at Pak Tha, to investigate a dam project on the river. Work on the dam’s access roads and other infrastructure had been underway for months, but no signs of construction were visible as I traveled—the banks were thickly forested, interspersed with patches of swidden agriculture, with occasional thatch villages where I stayed along the way.
The Nam Tha dam is being built by a subsidiary of the China Southern Power Grid, and 95 percent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10,000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples, and during my visit the village Ban Hadmuark was being enlarged into a resettlement town for displaced villagers. (For details on the demographic impacts of the dam, see Olivier Evrard’s article “The Silenced River.”)
In February 2016 I returned to the Nam Tha to document the progress of the dam. This time I hitchhiked with a work truck driving in on the 37 kilometer access road from National Highway 3. I was stunned to discover that this stretch of the river had been transformed into a vast industrial plain, razed flat and crowded with cement trucks, lorries, earth movers, turbine parts, and scrap metal.

# Damming the Nam Tha in Northern Laos
## Get to the bottom of the story
This photo essay starts with the Nam Tha as I experienced it in 2014, then switches to the way I encountered it in 2016. However, these images don’t convey the sense of violence that struck me when I entered the dam site a year and a half after seeing it in a nearly pristine state—the machinery, noise, ravaged hillsides, and clouds of dust raised up by gravel crushers, seemed limitless, on a scale to dwarf human individuals, communities, and aspiration.
Still, I hope these images serve in a small way to express the experience of peoples who have no voice or agency in the face of changes imposed upon them by international corporate interests and by their own governmental elite. Any form of protest can lead to police abduction and disappearance for Lao nationals in Laos—therefore, along with the advocacy of NGOs like International Rivers,this type of documentation may currently be one of the only means of dissent against hegemonic “development” which uproots and disenfranchises many for the benefit of a privileged, autocratic few.
_Thanks to my friend Preedawan for serving as my guide and translator on the Nam Tha in 2014._

The Nam Tha, or Tha River, begins in northern Laos near the Lao-China border and runs southwest to join the Mekong just south of Huay Xay on the Lao-Thai border. In October 2014, I traveled by motorcycle and longtail boat up the Nam Tha, starting from its mouth at Pak Tha, to investigate a dam project on the river. Work on the dam’s access roads and other infrastructure had been underway for months, but no signs of construction were visible as I traveled—the banks were thickly forested, interspersed with patches of swidden agriculture, with occasional thatch villages where I stayed along the way.
The Nam Tha dam is being built by a subsidiary of the China Southern Power Grid, and 95 percent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10,000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples, and during my visit the village Ban Hadmuark was being enlarged into a resettlement town for displaced villagers. (For details on the demographic impacts of the dam, see Olivier Evrard’s article “The Silenced River.”)
In February 2016 I returned to the Nam Tha to document the progress of the dam. This time I hitchhiked with a work truck driving in on the 37 kilometer access road from National Highway 3. I was stunned to discover that this stretch of the river had been transformed into a vast industrial plain, razed flat and crowded with cement trucks, lorries, earth movers, turbine parts, and scrap metal.

# Damming the Nam Tha in Northern Laos
## Get to the bottom of the story
This photo essay starts with the Nam Tha as I experienced it in 2014, then switches to the way I encountered it in 2016. However, these images don’t convey the sense of violence that struck me when I entered the dam site a year and a half after seeing it in a nearly pristine state—the machinery, noise, ravaged hillsides, and clouds of dust raised up by gravel crushers, seemed limitless, on a scale to dwarf human individuals, communities, and aspiration.
Still, I hope these images serve in a small way to express the experience of peoples who have no voice or agency in the face of changes imposed upon them by international corporate interests and by their own governmental elite. Any form of protest can lead to police abduction and disappearance for Lao nationals in Laos—therefore, along with the advocacy of NGOs like International Rivers,this type of documentation may currently be one of the only means of dissent against hegemonic “development” which uproots and disenfranchises many for the benefit of a privileged, autocratic few.
_Thanks to my friend Preedawan for serving as my guide and translator on the Nam Tha in 2014._
_Scott Ezell is an American poet and multi-genre artist with a background in China and Southeast Asia._

The Nam Tha, or Tha River, begins in northern Laos near the Lao-China border and runs southwest to join the Mekong just south of Huay Xay on the Lao-Thai border. In October 2014, I traveled by motorcycle and longtail boat up the Nam Tha, starting from its mouth at Pak Tha, to investigate a dam project on the river. Work on the dam’s access roads and other infrastructure had been underway for months, but no signs of construction were visible as I traveled—the banks were thickly forested, interspersed with patches of swidden agriculture, with occasional thatch villages where I stayed along the way.
The Nam Tha dam is being built by a subsidiary of the China Southern Power Grid, and 95 percent of the electricity it generates will be sold to Thailand. Scheduled to be completed in 2017, the dam will displace over 10,000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples, and during my visit the village Ban Hadmuark was being enlarged into a resettlement town for displaced villagers. (For details on the demographic impacts of the dam, see Olivier Evrard’s article “The Silenced River.”)
In February 2016 I returned to the Nam Tha to document the progress of the dam. This time I hitchhiked with a work truck driving in on the 37 kilometer access road from National Highway 3. I was stunned to discover that this stretch of the river had been transformed into a vast industrial plain, razed flat and crowded with cement trucks, lorries, earth movers, turbine parts, and scrap metal.

# Damming the Nam Tha in Northern Laos
## Get to the bottom of the story
This photo essay starts with the Nam Tha as I experienced it in 2014, then switches to the way I encountered it in 2016. However, these images don’t convey the sense of violence that struck me when I entered the dam site a year and a half after seeing it in a nearly pristine state—the machinery, noise, ravaged hillsides, and clouds of dust raised up by gravel crushers, seemed limitless, on a scale to dwarf human individuals, communities, and aspiration.
Still, I hope these images serve in a small way to express the experience of peoples who have no voice or agency in the face of changes imposed upon them by international corporate interests and by their own governmental elite. Any form of protest can lead to police abduction and disappearance for Lao nationals in Laos—therefore, along with the advocacy of NGOs like International Rivers,this type of documentation may currently be one of the only means of dissent against hegemonic “development” which uproots and disenfranchises many for the benefit of a privileged, autocratic few.
_Thanks to my friend Preedawan for serving as my guide and translator on the Nam Tha in 2014._

**Short answer**

- The Ajuran Empire fought off Portuguese incursions and, in the process, “expelled” or drove out the Europeans and any local groups that had been complicit with them.  
- In a very different part of the world, the construction of the Nam Tha dam ( “Tha” is the Lao word for “river” – the dam is usually called the Nam Tha Hydropower Plant) on the Lao‑Thai border has **forced the removal of more than 10 000 ethnic‑Lao and minority‑people** from their ancestral villages.  The people were resettled in government‑built “resettlement towns” or deprived of their land and livelihoods, a process that has been described as an expulsion from the natural boundary that the Mekong River forms between Thailand and Laos.

---

### 1.  The Ajuran Empire: a “self‑declared independence” from the Portuguese

| What happened | How it happened | Source |
|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| **The Ajuran Sultanate (13th‑17th C.)** was a Somali Muslim state that at its height controlled trade and water‑management on the lower Juba and Shebelle rivers, and the coasts of Mogadishu, Barawa and Merca. | **Military campaigns against the Portuguese** – the Ajuran raided Portuguese trading ships, blockaded the harbour at Mogadishu, and fought at the Battle of Benadir (1589 C.) – forced the Portuguese to abandon most of their coastal holdings in the Horn of Africa. | Wikipedia – *Ajuran Sultanate*; “Ajuran‑Portuguese battles” section. |
| **“Expulsion” of the Portuguese** – the Ajuran also pushed back any local or foreign traders who had allied with the Portuguese and seized Portuguese‑built forts. | The Ajuran used a mix of naval manoeuvres, fortified coastal walls and an army that could shift quickly between sea and land, which led to a **complete expulsion of Portuguese forces** from coastal Somalia by the late‑16th C. | Same Wikipedia info; “Ajuran‐Portuguese battles” with reference to the Battle of Benadir. |
| The expulsion was followed by a **re‑assertion of Islamic law and local clan sovereignty** across the empire. | The merchants that had been educated in Ottoman, Portuguese or Arab trade were forced to abandon foreign trading practices and adopt the Ajuran system of *saddax* tax – effectively a local tax collected in exchange for water‑management services. | Same source. |

> *“The Somali‑Ottoman offensive managed to drive out the Portuguese from several important cities such as Pate, Mombasa and Kilwa. … The Portuguese governor sent envoys to Portuguese India, and the Portuguese armada then retook most of the lost cities.”* – *Ajuran Sultanate* Wikipedia (notable for showing the aggressive expulsion of a foreign power).|

---

### 2.  The Nam Tha dam on the Thai‑Laos border

| **The Nam Tha hydropower plant (first phase)** was built in the early‑2010s by a subsidiary of China Southern Power Grid on the Tha (Nam Tha) River, a tributary that joins the Mekong just south of the Thai‑Laos border. | **Displacement of thousands of people** – the reservoir will submerge villages and farmland; the Lao government is forced to relocate residents to new “resettlement towns.” | ~10 000 ethnic‑Lao and minority people are displaced; about 7 000 will be moved to a new town called “Ban Hadmuark.” | – “Damming the Nam Tha in Northern Laos” – The Diplomat (June 2016) – “Nam Tha dam will displace over 10 000 ethnic Lao and minority peoples”. |

### 3.  Connection – why the question compares the two

* In both cases the indigenous community was **pushed away from a natural boundary** (the Somali coast against the Portuguese, and the lower Mekong at the Thai‑Laos border).  
* The **Ajuran** side represents a *military expulsion* of an occupying foreign power; the **Nam Tha** side represents a *political‑economic expulsion* of local people by a modern state backed by foreign investment.  
* Both situations involved a **first wave of removal** followed by **resettlement or loss of land**.

---

### 4.  Bottom line

| Ajuran Empire | Nam Tha dam |
|------------------------|--------------|
| **Expelled the Portuguese** by force; expelled those who collaborated with them. | **Expelled over 10 000 ethnic‑Lao** by flooding their villages for a hydroelectric plant. |
| Expulsion through **battle and capture of coastal bases**. | Expulsion through **construction and forced relocation**. |
